name: Mederma / onion extract scar gel

lead: Mederma is a widely sold gel containing onion bulb extract, used on surgical, injury, burn and acne scars to make them softer and less visible.

The maker describes moisturizing, cell renewal and collagen support, and onion flavonoids show anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies. Trials include a randomized comparison with a petrolatum emollient on new surgical scars, and results across studies are mixed.

paras: People rub a small amount onto healed skin daily, usually for weeks to months, often alongside silicone sheets, massage or sun protection on the scar. Forum posters also try it on old pockmarks.
It is for external use on healed skin, away from eyes and open wounds, per labelling. No serious adverse events are described in the sources reviewed.

web.title: Mederma / onion extract scar gel — Grokipedia

angle.text: Users apply this over-the-counter onion extract gel daily to surgical, burn and acne scars so they soften and fade, and some forum posters use it on old pockmarks. Trials against plain emollients have given mixed results.

lead: Mederma is an over-the-counter brand of topical scar products whose best-known product, Mederma Advanced Scar Gel, contains an extract of onion bulb (Allium cepa) together with other ingredients such as allantoin. It is marketed for improving the appearance of scars from surgery, injury, burns and acne.[1]

The brand was introduced in the United States in 1997 by Merz Pharmaceuticals and later passed to HRA Pharma (2019) and then Perrigo, according to one AI-generated encyclopedia summary.[1] Manufacturer claims of visible improvement in scar texture, colour and softness after weeks to months of daily use are described there.[1]

Published evidence is limited and mixed. A randomized, double-blind comparison of onion extract gel with a petrolatum-based emollient on new surgical scars has been published,[2] a rabbit-ear scar model study examined the product,[3] and several small trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.[4][5][6] Clinical references such as Wikipedia describe silicone, pressure, massage and steroid injection as the more commonly discussed scar treatments, and mention onion extract mainly as a comparator.[7]
infobox: Onion bulb extract (Cepalin), with allantoin and other additives[1]
Appearance of surgical, injury, burn and acne scars

paras: The flagship product is a water-based gel applied once daily to healed skin. The maker describes a three-part action of retaining moisture, supporting cell renewal and supporting collagen formation, and recommends roughly 8 weeks of use on new scars and 3 to 6 months on older ones.[1] Other products under the brand include an overnight cream, an SPF cream and a children's gel.[1]
The extract in the gel is described as containing flavonoids such as quercetin and kaempferol, which laboratory literature associates with anti-inflammatory activity.[1]

A prospective, double-blinded study compared an onion extract gel with a petrolatum-based emollient on new surgical scars; its introduction notes that few data had previously substantiated the product's claims.[2] The published conclusions are commonly summarized as showing no clear advantage of the gel over the emollient, while other trials are said to report improvement in scar appearance, hence the mixed picture described in secondary sources.[1][2]

The rabbit hypertrophic scar model study is an animal experiment, not a human trial; its abstract states that little scientific evidence supported the product at the time despite its widespread clinical use.[3]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed 20-person trial of Mederma on post-surgical scars (started 2012),[4] a completed phase 4 randomized comparison of two topical therapies for keloids and hypertrophic scars (30 participants, started 2006),[5] and a completed 75-person study of over-the-counter scar-management products (started 2019).[6]

In appearance-focused communities the product is mentioned as an inexpensive, widely stocked option for acne and surgical scars. The brand says it is the most recommended by doctors and pharmacists in the United States, based on surveys it cites.[1] Ownership changed from Merz to HRA Pharma in 2019 and to Perrigo thereafter.[1]
